subject: Agriculture
title: Orphan Crops Get Attention
description: A tiny lesson with a big payoff: Orphan Crops Get Attention.

hook.text: Teff, fonio, enset—crops feeding millions in Africa—have received almost zero modern breeding attention.

buildup.text: Global agriculture focused on wheat, rice, corn, and soybeans. Hundreds of nutritious crops were neglected.

discovery.text: The African Orphan Crops Consortium is sequencing genomes of 101 underutilized African food crops.

twist.text: Teff—Ethiopia's staple grain—is gluten-free and mineral-rich. It's now trendy in Western health food markets.

climax.text: Improving orphan crops helps the poorest farmers directly, since they already grow and eat these species.

punchline.text: The future of food isn't only new crops. It's old crops, finally improved.

quiz.question: What is the African Orphan Crops Consortium doing?
options: Sequencing genomes of 101 underutilized African food crops

details.summary: Orphan crops are nutritious, locally important species that have received little scientific research or breeding investment. This topic covers why crops like teff, fonio, and cowpea are finally gaining attention as climate-resilient food sources.
details.whyItMatters: Global agriculture depends on just three crops—rice, wheat, and corn—for 60% of calories. Investing in orphan crops diversifies food systems and builds resilience against climate shocks.
takeaways: Orphan crops include teff, fonio, cowpea, yam, and dozens of indigenous species
Many orphan crops are naturally drought-tolerant and nutrient-dense
Genomic sequencing is accelerating breeding programs for previously neglected species

faq.question: What are orphan crops and why are they called that?
faq.answer: Orphan crops are food plants that are locally important but have been 'orphaned' by the global research system—receiving minimal investment in breeding, agronomy, or market development compared to major commercial crops like corn and wheat.

faq.question: Why are orphan crops becoming important for food security?
faq.answer: Many orphan crops thrive in harsh conditions where major crops fail. As climate change stresses food systems, their resilience, nutritional diversity, and adaptation to local environments make them increasingly valuable for future food security.
